abstract.t: This document specifies the Secure Transport Communication Protocol (STCP). Its intended status is Standards Track. This initial draft records verified implementation behavior and identifies remaining interoperability and security specification work.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: STCP is a transport protocol with compact framing, X25519 key establishment, and AES-256-GCM-protected data and control messages. The wire version is distinct from the product version.

section.name: Wire Format
section.t: Each frame starts with a 17-octet header. Octet 0 is the descriptor: bits 0-3 packet type, bits 4-5 wire version (3), and bits 6-7 flags. Octets 1-4 contain the payload length; octets 5-8 the sequence; octets 9-12 the acknowledgment; and octets 13-16 the connection ID. All multioctet integers are big-endian.

Packet types are PublicKey (1), HandshakeDone (2), DataChunk (3), DataChunkEnd (4), Ack (5), Ping (6), Pong (7), Close (8), and Reset (9). PublicKey has a 64-octet payload; HandshakeDone has no payload. The implementation rejects unknown versions and packet types.

section.name: Handshake and State Transitions
section.t: The implementation states are New, Bound, Listening, Handshake, Ready, Closed, and Error. The handshake procedures described below are observed in the 2026-11-02 Linux source snapshot; complete wire-level error semantics are not yet standardized.

li.t: When a connection enters Handshake with an attached carrier, the local endpoint sends a PublicKey frame. Its 64-octet payload contains the local 32-octet X25519 public key in octets 0 through 31. The current Linux implementation initializes the remaining 32 octets to zero. The PublicKey frame advertises the COMPRESSION_CAPABLE flag.

On receiving a PublicKey frame, the implementation requires a 64-octet payload and rejects flags other than COMPRESSION_CAPABLE. It derives directional traffic keys from the peer public key and sends an empty HandshakeDone frame.

The receiver permits HandshakeDone to arrive before PublicKey and remembers its receipt. The handshake parser stops before consuming subsequent application DATA when the required handshake inputs are present.

The local connection transitions to Ready only when local traffic keys have been derived and a peer HandshakeDone has been received. An established application DATA frame must not be interpreted as a handshake frame.

section.t: PublicKey and HandshakeDone are not protected by the established-session DATA or control authentication mechanism. In particular, HandshakeDone does not prove the peer's identity or cryptographically bind the full handshake transcript. The base protocol does not authenticate peer identity.

section.name: Directional Key Derivation
section.t: The active Linux key derivation takes the 32-octet X25519 shared secret, the 32-octet client public key, and the 32-octet server public key, in that role-defined order. It computes:

li.t: client_to_server_key = HMAC-SHA256(key=PRK, message=ASCII("STCPv4 AES256-GCM client to server key") || 0x01).
server_to_client_key = HMAC-SHA256(key=PRK, message=ASCII("STCPv4 AES256-GCM server to client key") || 0x01).
For each direction, control_key = HMAC-SHA256(key=directional_data_key, message=ASCII("STCP wire3 control AES256-GCM key") || 0x01).

section.t: ASCII strings do not include a terminating NUL octet. The client uses the client-to-server key for transmission and the server-to-client key for reception; the server uses the reverse assignment. The reviewed code rejects identical directional keys. A separate STCPv2 derivation helper exists in the source tree but is not invoked by this reviewed Linux session-key path. Cross-platform equivalence and deterministic known-answer vectors remain to be verified.

section.name: Packet Protection
section.t: DATA uses AES-256-GCM with the encoded 17-octet header as additional authenticated data, an 8-octet transmitted nonce, and a 16-octet tag. The 12-octet GCM IV is four zero octets followed by the big-endian transmitted nonce. Control packets Ack, Ping, Pong, Close, and Reset use a separate derived control key and authenticate the header with a tag over empty plaintext. A 64-position replay window rejects duplicate authenticated control nonces.

section.name: Authenticated Packet Layout and Replay Handling
section.t: For encrypted DATA, the 17-octet encoded header is AES-GCM additional authenticated data (AAD). The frame carries an 8-octet big-endian nonce followed by ciphertext and a 16-octet authentication tag. The 12-octet GCM IV is 0x00000000 || nonce. Reliable retransmission reuses the original stored encrypted frame bytes instead of encrypting altered plaintext under the same nonce.

A protected control frame (Ack, Ping, Pong, Close, or Reset) uses a distinct directional control key, its encoded header as AAD, an 8-octet nonce, and a 16-octet authentication tag over empty plaintext. After tag verification, the receiver applies a 64-position sliding replay window: duplicates and values at least 64 behind the greatest accepted nonce are rejected. In-order DATA delivery also checks the expected sequence and nonce after authentication; authenticated out-of-order DATA can be buffered.
These observations do not establish nonce uniqueness across every reconnect, failure, alternate carrier, or key-lifecycle path.

section.name: Reliability, Acknowledgments and Retransmission
section.t: The following values describe the reviewed Linux implementation rather than negotiated protocol parameters. Reliability is enabled when the carrier reports that STCP reliability is required; the TCP carrier does not run the STCP retransmission timer.

section.name: Send Window and Segmentation
section.t: The implementation uses a fixed maximum of eight outstanding reliable DATA frames per connection. An application send that would exceed the pending-frame limit returns a retry indication instead of adding the frames. Application data is split into DataChunk frames, with DataChunkEnd marking the last frame of a send. This limit is a frame-count bound, not a receiver-advertised congestion window.

section.name: Cumulative ACK Processing
section.t: ACK values are cumulative. On receipt of a valid authenticated ACK with acknowledgment number A, the sender removes pending frames whose sequence numbers are less than or equal to A. An ACK referring to a sequence not yet transmitted is treated as a protocol error. The receiver normally sends an ACK after four received frames; selected events can force an earlier ACK. Duplicate-ACK recovery can resend the latest cumulative acknowledgment. When acknowledged frames release pending capacity, blocked senders are awakened.

section.name: Round-Trip Time Estimation
section.t: The initial retransmission timeout (RTO) is 60 milliseconds. The timer tick is 20 milliseconds, and the RTO is clamped between 20 and 3000 milliseconds. An RTT sample is collected only from a frame that has not been retransmitted, avoiding ambiguous samples as in Karn's algorithm. On the first sample R, SRTT is R and RTTVAR is max(1, floor(R/2)). On subsequent samples, RTTVAR becomes floor((3*RTTVAR + abs(SRTT-R))/4) and SRTT becomes floor((7*SRTT + R)/8). RTO becomes clamp(SRTT + 4*RTTVAR, 20, 3000) milliseconds. These integer formulas reflect the current implementation.

section.name: Retransmission Timer
section.t: For each pending frame, the implementation maintains an age in timer ticks, a per-frame RTO and a retry count. On expiry it resends the stored encrypted frame bytes without generating a new nonce. Per-frame RTO doubles after a retransmission, capped at 3000 milliseconds. No more than four pending frames are selected for retransmission per timer tick. After eight retries for a pending frame, the connection reports a terminal timeout corresponding to ETIMEDOUT. The implementation updates retransmission and timeout counters.

section.name: Congestion-Control Limitations
section.t: The fixed eight-frame outstanding limit and four-retransmissions-per-tick bound limit bursts, but do not establish a complete Internet congestion-control algorithm. No standards-conformant congestion response to sustained loss, fairness mechanism, or explicit receiver-advertised flow-control window has yet been verified from the reviewed source. Deployment over shared Internet paths requires further congestion-control design and validation before this draft can claim Standards Track readiness.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Because the base handshake lacks peer identity authentication, an active man-in-the-middle can substitute public keys. AES-GCM protection after key establishment does not prevent this attack. Nonce uniqueness, session-key freshness, reconnect behavior, and cross-platform interoperability require further verification. The connection ID is not an authentication credential.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This initial version requests no allocation. IP protocol number 253 is experimental and is not a permanent STCP assignment. Native IP carriage and any permanent protocol-number request require further specification.

section.name: Outstanding Work
section.t: Before Standards Track publication, the draft needs complete normative state-machine and error rules, independent KDF test vectors, carrier mapping, compression negotiation, congestion control, security review, and interoperability evidence. This document does not claim IETF approval.
